<reason>CON built a single sustained thesis — that a ban only binds compliant states while a liability/testing regime improves outcomes unilaterally — and defended it under real pressure. CON turned PRO's own cluster-munitions example into evidence for non-compliance, forced a genuine dilemma on "meaningful human control" (either the ban is toothless on target-class readings, or it bans exactly the useful edge case), and answered PRO's sharpest pressure question (why doesn't asymmetry sink liability too?) with a clean distinction: liability works domestically without treaty cooperation, prohibition's entire value depends on universal compliance. PRO never fully dislodged that distinction; its closing repeated "prevention beats litigation" without directly re-engaging the unilateral/multilateral point, and its "bite the bullet" answer to the squeeze (banning classification of unknown contacts is "the ban working") conceded the very narrowness CON was pressing on. PRO's accountability and moral-judgment arguments were solid and its definition of meaningful human control was genuinely clarifying, but CON's rebuttals landed with more force and were less answered. CON's two speeches being clipped for length is a real execution cost, though the core arguments were delivered before the cut.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A1 in Rebuttal 2 — answering PRO's pressure question by distinguishing that strict liability/testing regimes deliver benefits unilaterally (no treaty needed) while a ban's entire value depends on universal compliance — decisively defused PRO's tu quoque that both regimes share the same enforcement asymmetry, and PRO's closing never fully recovered from it.</best_rebuttal>
